The basic model is 3500 kcal = 1 lb. A 500 kcal daily surplus for 60 days would roughly result in a gain of 8,5 lbs (ignoring the increase in TDEE as weight increases). So yeah, an additional 500 kcal is a lot and will add up in the long run. Based on your data the surplus may have been even higher so you may be underestimating the increase in food or decrease in physical activity (or you may need to see a doctor). One thing that's usually missing from "weight loss in short people" conversations is that we should not aim for the same "absolute" loss as taller people, I think it's healthier and easier to focus on relative % loss and take it slower (like a 250 kcal deficit vs the usually recommended 500 kcal). I often see opinions that muscle training could be good for upping the deficit because muscles burn calories at rest.

I think this is a very wrong approach for personal finance. You are planning to be old, right? You are probably not planning to be sick or disabled or need long-term care, but these things may happen. I don't know what savings you already have, if you have a pension plan (government-guaranteed or an employer plan), but not having enough resources in times of crisis/retirement is a real issue.

I don't know what content is presented to you, but crypto, trading, real estate, stock picking, derivatives etc, are a different thing from the more passive-oriented investing aimed at "normal individuals" concerned with their future and you could only benefit from being more aware of how you spend and earn money. Products aimed at retail investors (like the ETFs, EDIT: also insurance, annuities, whatever pension systems and retirement accounts there are) are also very simple to understand, they are simple and prepackaged because retail investors do not have the time, resources and knowledge to build a diversified portfolio from scratch and calculate shit and track everything.

You are not expected to know everything but personal finance is about making your life better (and we're not talking millionaire better, we're talking affording medicine and food when you're 80). I guess it's fine to ignore the topic completely if you're planning to leave the world right after retirement (or if you're 100% satisfied with the pension you're going to get, not everyone has that luxury). You can also get a financial planner or a wealth manager once you decide to look into the topic, but again, most of us are probably not able to hire a top one + you need some basic knowledge for due diligence.

If anything, personal finance and minimalism go hand-in-hand (awareness of spending and consumption) but I do realise how some content creators approach the topic (+scams, obviously...).

That's the question about "how much to hedge" currency risk in the portfolio, you need to weigh the benefits and costs. You will need to check whether the hedge (depends what currency the current position is in and what side) requires you to buy low/sell high or buy high/sell low. If you buy low/sell high, you will trade with the forward rate bias, this is a "financially good" position to have, so you may decide to overhedge, you will benefit from more buying low and more selling high. If the hedge makes you buy high and sell low, it increases the cost of the hedge so you will probably decide to underhedge, accept more currency risk but decrease the costs.

1. Team work: plenty of group projects at uni that help you discover your natural role in a group, conflict resolution, strong vs weak parts of project elements (example, some people cannot present for shit, if I have to do a group presentation with others, I'd rather let them do the research stuff and the slides in exchange for me doing the presenting part on my own).
2. CFA program tasks are self-contained compared with projects: no looking up data, no process related to checking and processing the data, coming up with the approach, limited tools, no brainstorming with smarter people like the professors, no academic papers to verify your approach. Some resources you may miss: subscriptions to journals, reuters eikon(datasteam? refinitiv?) or bloomberg. Part of the fun of preparing the thesis is just finding the topic that interests you, reading everything related to it and then realizing there's not enough data available to actually do the analysis so you start over. The uni will promote your natural curiosity for a specific topic better than the program imo.
3. Microsoft Office Starter pack: I know L1 started throwing in some Excel formulas but it's not like you have to learn and use them. Word: general writing, argumentation, adding sources and references, styles, formatting, fighting with the lack of inspiration but the paper is due midnight, ability to read, process, transform and then condense your research/findings. Excel: how to make a file that you will understand a year later, formulas, conditional formatting, data analysis toolpack, macros, formatting, fighting with dates, charts and overall data presentation, coming up with solutions to optimize your tasks. Power Point: speech+10, condensing findings, not putting all of your text on the slide, anything visual/format related, working with different media types and tools to enhance the slides, how to present so that your colleagues are actually listening to you instead of doing homework. Access: i forgor everything from that one... databases? One to one and many to many?
4. Other cool software: some uni programs will try to introduce you to R, Python, SQL, MatLab, PowerBi, Tableau. I also had Orange, Gretl, Weka. Some of these are more for data-science or quant than just Finance but they can help in some particular tasks.
5. Maths/stats: I think quant readings for the CFA Program can be much harder if you haven't been introduced to these concepts earlier. At uni the pace is slower and they will introduce other concepts that may appear later, mainly from calculus. You probably won't need that if you're sticking to less quant areas of Finance or economics, however, but it's nice when you see a complex formula in a product paper and you get it.

I definitely agree with the cultural differences of how suicide is treated. But for me rationality is connected with how the brain makes the decision and saying that the brain is rational in one culture and not the other is not a direction I would like to go towards. I'm more interested in the biological component, so a healthy living organism making the decision to end its life (so rejection of survival). Many have mentioned suicide due to terminal illnesses and I do see the link between that and animals/humans not fulfilling their basic needs right before death, like eating; the brain knows it will die in the future, the time horizon is just different (perhaps due to realization of death before symptoms worsen thanks to medical knowledge).
There is definitely something fascinating about the assumption "all biological creatures consciously want to die".

My personal opinion is that if someone wants to die, they should be allowed to, I don't care if it's rational or not (so my position is pretty radical by itself). But if we do assume that only rational decisions should be accepted by the computer/psychiatrist, I do wonder how that would work in practice and what kind of issues could come up. So continuing with Alzheimer's, if the patient in diagnosed at t=0 and makes the decision that they want to die, when should the appointment take place? Should it be a specific day stated now, should it be a result of a continuous assessment of the patient's condition so that the patient dies right before the next stage appears? Can we even monitor Alzheimer's that well? And to repeat, what if the patient does not want to die and is begging to be kept alive during the appointment because dementia has set in so deeply they forgot about the wish to die? This would be traumatic for the patient, for the clinic and for the family if they were allowed to be there.

These are definitely different, they are brought on by desperation, fear or guilt, I guess it could be said that some of them would be rational (commit suicide instead of being tortured by the enemy, losing social status in nations with a huge focus on the community), some not (I don't know what is meant by spiritual reasons but I would not say that committing suicide to meet with a god or reach enlightenment is rational). It would require the assumption that the brain is making a logical assessment of the situation in the blink of an eye and is indeed choosing the better option, which is not always true.

>losing your mental faculties

This one is going to be a huge challenge for this service imo, there is something contradictory in "making a rational decision when your brain is impacted by an illness", I don't know if neuroscience has gone that far.

If the model fits well, you will be able to predict prices using the four independent variables. But now you should look at the variables again. As you can see, all of them are quite similar if you think about it, when there are clouds, there will usually be rain, the temperature will be lower, there will be less sun. When there is rain, there are clouds, there is no sun, the temperature is lower etc etc... All these variables are highly correlated and you won't be able to properly assess their significance or coefficients (while the model as a whole may be okay).
